question:
Patient note:
A 41-year-old man lies in the pre-operative holding bay awaiting transfer to the operating theatre for a planned four-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy to treat a symptomatic gallbladder full of stones that has caused two bouts of biliary colic during the current admission; the general-surgery team estimates 90 – 120 minutes of pneumoperitoneum with an anticipated overnight stay on the surgical ward. He has spent the last five hospital days almost entirely supine because persistent right-upper-quadrant pain worsens when he sits or stands, and nursing flow-sheets document fewer than two assisted trips to the bedside commode in each 12-hour shift. Two and a half weeks before this admission he rolled his left ankle while stepping off a ladder; radiographs confirmed the absence of fracture, yet orthopaedics applied a below-knee fiberglass cast to protect a partial tear of the peroneus brevis tendon. The cast remains in place today, extending from just distal to the tibial tuberosity to the metatarsal heads, and his toes are warm and pink with brisk capillary refill. Apart from the immobilised limb, physical examination shows prominent, tortuous superficial veins coursing along both gastrocnemius bellies—changes he first noticed as a teenager when working long shifts in a warehouse—and there is no pitting oedema or discrepancy in calf circumference. He has never experienced cramping calf pain, unexplained dyspnoea, or radiologically confirmed clot in the legs or lungs, and no first-degree relative has reported such events. A year ago he underwent an evaluation for an incidentally prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time discovered during employment screening; the coagulation laboratory detected circulating antiphospholipid antibodies on two occasions twelve weeks apart, and haematology counselled him on the risks of thrombosis but elected against chronic anticoagulation in the absence of prior clinical events. He denies bowel disorders, chronic lung disease, prior admissions for heart-failure decompensation, recent systemic infections, or exposure to long-term intravenous catheters. The current episode represents his first hospitalisation in more than a decade, and he has not undergone any operative or endoscopic procedure within the last thirty days. Review of systems is negative for fever, productive cough, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, chest tightness, palpitations, transient neurologic deficits, or visual changes. He quit smoking nine years ago after a 15-pack-year history, drinks one or two beers on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Home medications consist solely of over-the-counter ibuprofen for musculoskeletal aches and a daily multivitamin; he does not take glucocorticoids, selective oestrogen-receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or platelet inhibitors. On examination this morning he rests comfortably in a semi-recumbent position, answers questions lucidly, and is oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 126/72 mm Hg, heart rate 74 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air; body mass index is 27 kg m⁻². Jugular venous contour is below the sternal angle with the head elevated to 30°, the apical impulse is nondisplaced, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and lung fields are clear bilaterally with full excursion. The abdomen is soft and mildly tender beneath the right costal margin without guarding or rebound, bowel sounds are present, and no organomegaly is appreciated. The left lower leg cast is intact with no foul odour or drainage; capillary refill in the exposed toes is under two seconds, and posterior tibial as well as dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable 2+ bilaterally. The right leg, free of immobilisation, displays the same network of dilated superficial veins but no erythema, cords, or swelling. Neurologic screen reveals intact cranial nerves and 5/5 strength in all uncasted muscle groups. A single 18-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter in the right forearm is patent and running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no midline, PICC, or implanted port is present. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn at 05:30 show haemoglobin 14.2 g dL⁻¹, haematocrit 43 %, platelets 238 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.93 mg dL⁻¹, AST 22 U L⁻¹, ALT 24 U L⁻¹, alkaline phosphatase 118 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 1.1 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 39 s, consistent with his known inhibitor. A standard 12-lead electrocardiogram reviewed by anaesthesia shows normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats min⁻¹, normal axis, and no acute ST-T changes. Overnight abdominal ultrasonography confirmed multiple echogenic calculi with acoustic shadowing, a modestly thickened gallbladder wall, and a patent common bile duct measuring 5 mm. An upright chest radiograph obtained yesterday depicts clear lungs and an unremarkable mediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, inter-incisor distance of 4 cm, and full cervical extension. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves encircle both calves but have not yet been activated, and prophylactic anticoagulation is on hold until final surgical sign-in.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums weighted perioperative VTE risk factors. The BMI cutoff matters in this case.
1. Age 41 (age 41–60) → 1.
2. Visible varicose veins → 1.
3. Planned laparoscopic surgery lasting 90–120 minutes (>45 minutes) → 2.
4. Confined to bed for five days (>72 hours), apart from brief commode trips → 2.
5. Immobilizing lower-leg cast → 2.
6. Persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies (acquired thrombophilia) → 3. No personal or family VTE history adds points.
These factors sum to 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11. With an obesity cutoff of BMI ≥30, BMI 27 adds 0, leaving 11. The standard 2005 Caprini model uses BMI >25 and therefore gives 12 instead.
Final answer: 11
